pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words, answered about their own capstone with concrete numbers and committed evidence; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: State your performance goal as you wrote it before you touched any code: which operation, which input, what it cost, what you wanted.
expected_points: names an operation someone waits for, not an internal function that was convenient to benchmark
input size and shape taken from the PRD's non-functional requirements
a before number and a target number, both with units
one axis — latency, throughput or memory — because a goal with three has none
the target came from somewhere real: a perception threshold, a timeout, a memory limit, an SLO

questions.prompt: Walk me through how you found the bottleneck. What did you expect the profile to say, and what did it actually say?
expected_points: top-down: time the whole operation, then profile the layer that owns the time
chose the profile by symptom — CPU profile for busy, heap alloc_space for garbage, execution trace or block/mutex profile when the clock is long but the CPU is idle
reads flat versus cum correctly and used -list to get to specific lines
checked the share before the function: a 3% cost cannot pay back more than 3% (Amdahl)
can say where their intuition was wrong, which is the point of measuring first

questions.prompt: How do I know your optimization actually worked? Show me the numbers and tell me how you produced them.
expected_points: same benchmark, same inputs, same -count, same machine, before and after; both outputs committed
repeated runs (benchstat, or medians and ranges) — a single run each side is a coin flip
no -race while benchmarking; instrumentation distorts the ratios
benchstat's ~ means no detectable difference no matter what the means say
allocs/op and B/op quoted next to ns/op, because allocation counts survive other people's hardware

questions.prompt: Was your win algorithmic or constant-factor, and how does your data show it? Under what conditions is your headline number true?
expected_points: the size sweep answers it: parallel curves mean a constant-factor win, a collapsed ratio means the growth term changed
says which variable the cost tracks now (store size, matches, output length), not just 'it is faster'
a constant-factor win applied to the wrong algorithm gets thrown away when the algorithm is fixed
the claim carries its conditions: input size, selectivity or data shape, hardware, Go version

questions.prompt: What did this optimization cost, and why is that price acceptable here? What would make you undo it?
expected_points: a specific cost: readability, extra memory, an invariant now maintained in two places, a cache that can go stale, a new dependency
'no trade-off' is not an answer — at minimum the code is harder to read than the obvious version
the price is justified against the sizes in their PRD, not in the abstract
a concrete flip condition: the workload change or new feature that would make them revert

questions.prompt: How do you know behaviour did not change? Which test would fail if it had?
expected_points: names the tests, and they are the ones listed in PERF.md and run by the harness
existing tests were written against the code that was replaced, so passing them proves less than it feels like
a differential test keeps the old implementation as an oracle and compares over generated input
covers the corners optimizations break: empty input, duplicates, values needing normalisation, no match, concurrent access
fuzzing old against new, or golden files, where the input or output space is wide

questions.prompt: Name something in your project you deliberately did not optimize. Make the case with a number.
expected_points: a share from the profile, or a latency already inside the SLO
the win would sit inside measurement noise
the speed would be bought with correctness risk — cache staleness, a new race, an invariant split in two
the real fix is at a different layer: cache, batch, queue, or delete the work (S6 vocabulary)
the bottleneck is I/O or round trips, where a tuned Go loop changes nothing

questions.prompt: Talk about your capstone the way you would to a senior engineer joining the team: what it does, where the boundaries are, what breaks first, and what is wrong with it.
expected_points: what it does and who for, without describing the implementation
package boundaries and dependency direction, with the seam they would swap
numbers instead of adjectives for size, latency and memory, and how they know them
failure modes: what breaks first under load, what happens when a dependency is down, what the operator does
at least three known weaknesses, a decision they reversed with the evidence, and what they would cut under time pressure
the next bottleneck and how they would confirm it
